The method is used to evaluate a semiconductor wafer having a polished surface by means of a laser surface-inspection device. In this evaluation, the device directs incident light from a single incident optical system onto the polished surface of the semiconductor wafer.

When the incident light reaches the polished surface, radiation light is generated as a result of reflection or scattering from the surface. This radiation light is received by three separate light-receiving systems arranged to detect light from the wafer surface.

Based on the received radiation light, the method detects abnormalities present on or near the polished surface of the semiconductor wafer. Such abnormalities include, for example, process-induced defects and foreign matter adhered to the wafer surface. These abnormalities are detected as light point defects.

The three light-receiving systems are configured so that they are not all identical in their detection characteristics. Specifically, at least one of the light-receiving angle and the polarization selectivity differs among the three light-receiving systems. By using multiple receiving systems with different optical conditions, the method enables more detailed evaluation of light point defects on the polished surface of the semiconductor wafer.
outputs.L4:
A semiconductor wafer having a polished main surface is subjected to surface inspection using a laser surface-inspection apparatus. In this inspection, a beam of incident laser light is directed onto the polished surface of the wafer at a predetermined angle. When the laser light reaches the wafer surface, radiation is generated in the form of reflected light and scattered light. This radiation contains information about the condition of the wafer surface, including the presence of small defects, particles, or other irregularities.

The inspection apparatus includes three separate light-receiving systems for collecting the radiation produced from the irradiated portion of the wafer surface. These light-receiving systems are arranged so that they differ from one another in at least one optical condition, such as the angle at which light is received, the range of scattering directions being detected, or the polarization component of the received light. For example, one receiver may collect light in a relatively low-angle direction, another may collect light in a higher-angle direction, and a third may selectively receive a particular polarization component of the scattered or reflected radiation.

As the wafer is scanned by the incident laser beam, each light-receiving system produces a corresponding detection signal. These signals represent the intensity and optical characteristics of light returned from each inspected location on the wafer surface. A light point defect, such as a minute particle, a polishing-related defect, a crystal-originated defect, or a process-induced defect, changes the scattered-light pattern in a manner that depends on the nature of the defect. Accordingly, the signals obtained from the three receiving systems are compared with one another to evaluate the type and condition of the detected defect.

In particular, defects caused by wafer processing and foreign matter adhered to the wafer surface may produce different relationships among the detected signals. A particle attached to the surface may scatter light strongly in certain directions or polarization states, while a shallow surface defect, pit, scratch, or process-induced irregularity may exhibit a different angular or polarization-dependent scattering characteristic. By comparing the detection outputs from receivers having different light-receiving angles and/or polarization selectivity, the apparatus can distinguish between these different categories of light point defects more accurately than an inspection system using only a single receiver.

The method therefore provides an improved technique for evaluating the polished surface of a semiconductor wafer. It not only detects the presence and position of light point defects on the wafer surface, but also assists in classifying the defects according to their probable origin or physical nature. This enables more reliable discrimination between adhered foreign matter and process-induced defects, thereby improving quality control in semiconductor wafer manufacturing and subsequent device fabrication processes.

**A Method of Turning Ideas into Action**

A method of achieving any goal begins with clarity. Before progress can happen, it is important to understand what needs to be done, why it matters, and what outcome is expected. Whether the goal is learning a new skill, solving a problem, improving a business process, or completing a creative project, having a clear method helps transform an idea into practical action.

The first step is planning. A good plan breaks a large task into smaller, manageable parts. This makes the process less overwhelming and allows progress to be measured along the way. Each step should have a purpose, a deadline, and a clear connection to the final result.

The second step is consistency. Even the best method will not work without regular effort. Small actions performed consistently often lead to greater success than occasional bursts of intense work. By following a routine and staying focused, it becomes easier to build momentum and overcome obstacles.

The third step is evaluation. A method of improvement should include time to review what is working and what is not. Mistakes are not failures; they are useful information. By learning from results and making adjustments, the method becomes stronger and more effective.

Finally, persistence is essential. Most meaningful achievements take time. A reliable method provides structure, but determination keeps the process moving forward. When planning, consistency, evaluation, and persistence come together, almost any goal becomes more achievable.

**Formal Patent Language**

A method and apparatus are provided for evaluating a surface condition of a polished wafer. The method comprises directing laser radiation from a single incident optical system onto a surface of the polished wafer at a predetermined incident angle, thereby generating radiation scattered and/or reflected from the wafer surface. The generated radiation is received by a plurality of detector systems including first, second, and third detector systems. The detector systems are arranged to detect respective portions of the scattered and/or reflected radiation.

At least one of the detector systems is configured differently from another of the detector systems with respect to at least one optical detection parameter, the optical detection parameter including a receiving angle relative to the wafer surface, an azimuthal detection direction, a polarization condition, or a combination thereof. Output signals from the first, second, and third detector systems are compared with one another to determine characteristics of the polished wafer, including surface defects, haze, roughness, particles, scratches, polishing marks, or other surface non-uniformities.

In one embodiment, the apparatus includes a laser light source, an incident optical path configured to irradiate the wafer surface with the laser light, and three detector optical systems positioned to receive radiation scattered and/or reflected from the irradiated region of the wafer. The detector systems may include polarization-selective elements, angularly separated collection optics, or both, such that the detected signals provide distinguishable information regarding the wafer surface. A processing unit receives detection signals from the detector systems and evaluates the polished wafer based on a comparison, ratio, differential value, correlation, or other relationship among the detection signals.

**Exemplary Claim**

1. A method for evaluating a polished wafer, comprising:  
   directing laser light from a single incident optical system onto a surface of the polished wafer;  
   receiving radiation scattered or reflected from the surface by a first detector system;  
   receiving radiation scattered or reflected from the surface by a second detector system;  
   receiving radiation scattered or reflected from the surface by a third detector system; and  
   comparing detection signals obtained from the first, second, and third detector systems to evaluate a surface condition of the polished wafer,  
   wherein at least one of the first, second, and third detector systems differs from another of the detector systems in at least one of a receiving angle and a polarization condition.

2. The method of claim 1, wherein the surface condition comprises at least one of a particle, a scratch, haze, roughness, a polishing defect, and a surface non-uniformity.

3. The method of claim 1, wherein comparing the detection signals comprises determining at least one of a ratio, a difference, a weighted combination, or a correlation among the detection signals.

4. The method of claim 1, wherein at least one of the detector systems receives radiation having a polarization component different from a polarization component received by another of the detector systems.

5. The method of claim 1, wherein at least one of the detector systems is disposed at a receiving angle different from a receiving angle of another of the detector systems relative to the surface of the polished wafer.

6. An apparatus for evaluating a polished wafer, comprising:  
   a laser source;  
   an incident optical system configured to direct laser light from the laser source onto a surface of the polished wafer;  
   first, second, and third detector systems configured to receive radiation scattered or reflected from the surface; and  
   a processor configured to compare output signals from the first, second, and third detector systems to evaluate a surface condition of the polished wafer,  
   wherein at least one of the first, second, and third detector systems differs from another of the detector systems in at least one of a receiving angle and a polarization condition.
